languages.title: Heavy soft display type
languages.define: Cooper-style soft serifs, rounded sans and bubble letters: heavy, soft-edged, often touching, often larger than the panel that holds them.
read: The weight carries the appetite. Strokes thicken toward the middle of the letter as if filled, counters shrink to slits, terminals round off. Yellowbird's mark (229) climbs and leans so the word seems to be getting up; Bezi's (083) is stretched to fit the lid of its tub until the letters are the container. When the letters sag, as in Dally's wordmark (063) beside its translucent peach spheres, the lettering is doing what the food does.

The lineage runs from Cooper Black (1922) through its second life on 1960s and 70s record sleeves and supermarket shelves, and the board's version keeps that warmth without the distress: flat color, clean edges, a single offset outline at most (141). Where the letters are geometric and rounded rather than serifed (006, 010, 024, 125), the reference shifts a decade later, to the bubble lettering of children's television and cereal.

The relationship to the pack is the point. These marks are set large enough to be cropped by the panel (046, 108, 116), so the pack becomes a window onto a bigger word. The food, when it appears, sits below or behind. The letter is the hero and the product is the evidence.
languages.relations: Set against Condensed caps and label typography on nearly every pack. Refused by Reductive packaging. With Character illustration, the board's most common sign of warmth; the two rarely share a panel.

plates.caption: The mark climbs. Letters lean into each other and the baseline rises, so the word reads as a motion, not a label.
Lettering stretched to the lid's edge. The name becomes the container's shape; three colorways change nothing else.
The stems sag. Beside see-through jelly spheres, the letters take on the product's physics.

languages.title: Script lettering
languages.define: Joined or brush-made lettering: monoline, casual script, heavy upright script, swash.
read: Script is the board's second voice. It almost never carries the whole message; it sits over or beside a plainer face and supplies the tone. Lazy Sundays (150) puts a looping "Lazy" over fat rounded caps. Risotto (243) sets the product name in script above a bowl. Nooish (226) uses "Instant Classic!" in script as the aside inside a layout of bands. The script is the parenthesis.

Three sources are visible. The sign-painter's monoline (016, 155, 119) is quick and even, a brush that never stops. The soda-fountain script (228, 194) is heavier, upright and joined, a quotation of 1950s American refreshment. The hand-lettered display script (053, 009) has swash and swelling, closer to 1970s phototype. Which one a brand chooses sets its decade.

Because script implies a person writing, it does the work of a signature. Stiller's runs it up the can like a wall sign; SuperRico (016) is nothing but the script on red, which is enough to be a brand.
languages.relations: Almost always the second voice beside Condensed caps and label typography. Shares the habit of quotation with Grocery vernacular devices.

languages.title: Condensed caps and label typography
languages.define: Narrow capitals and small typographic furniture: the voice of the tin label, the notice and the specimen sheet.
read: This is where facts live. Wood-type gothics and condensed grotesks carry flavor names (025, 034, 291), while small caps, typewriter and mono carry weight, count and origin (162, 305, 045). The register reads as honest because it is the type of things that are not designed: crate labels, price notices, specification sheets.

It has a poster mode too. The condensed serif stack (011, 139) sets a pep-talk sentence in a block, black on yellow, and the repetition of words becomes the rhythm of the image. Glossier's bodega notice (120) is the same idea in one ink on pink. The copy is plain; the setting makes it a picture.

Within a pack, this register is what makes the heavy soft display type legible as a brand. Juicy Marbles (291) sets "meat" enormous and the grams small; Heyday (301) sets the whole name in it and lets color do the rest. The difference between a loud pack and a quiet one on this board is mostly how much of the panel is given to this voice.
languages.relations: The counterweight to Heavy soft display type and Script lettering. Grocery vernacular devices supplies its shapes.

languages.title: Copy-led design
languages.define: A sentence set as the whole surface: the pep-talk poster, the talking pack, the billboard that says one thing.
read: A group of pins has no image except what the words say. "Have a really, really nice day" (011), "Good things happen when you try" (139), "Let's make things better" (122): second-person encouragement, set large, in a face that softens it. The lineage is the 1970s head-shop poster and the greeting card, and the tone is kind rather than clever.

On packs the same idea turns into a voice. Lazy Food (256, 257) repeats CHEESY behind its pouch and names itself for the effort it saves; Oatly (167) covers its carton in talk; Matty's (232) quotes its own instructions as if a friend were speaking. The pack addresses the buyer directly and the design steps back to let it.

What makes these work is restraint elsewhere. One face, one or two colors, and a sentence short enough to read from across a room (225, 264). When the copy has to share the surface with a photograph (302, 253), the letters are cut out or laid on as objects, so that the sentence stays a thing rather than a caption.
languages.relations: Borrows its faces from Condensed caps and label typography and Heavy soft display type. Where it meets a photograph it uses the cut-paper method of Cut-paper illustration.

languages.title: Type integrated with the food
languages.define: Type set in, on or as the food: letters made of liquid, words fitted to a fruit, a title that frames the dish.
read: Here the two halves of a pack, word and picture, become one thing. TOMATO (094) is set in a thin wide serif directly on a macro of sauce, so the word is read through the texture. BUBBLES (114) is spelled in water. Algae Cooking Club (134) is written in oil on steel. The letters stop being a label and become a property of the food.

A second version fits the word to the food's silhouette. Happy Chuseok (009) is drawn inside a fruit; NOMM (152) puts its letters inside a rolling pin and bowls; the SOUP ladle (158) pours its own name. These are rebus devices from sign painting and the 1960s poster, and they read fast because the shape is recognized before the word.

The third version uses the word as a frame. Lazy Nights (280, 336) sets its name enormous down the side of a noodle photograph; Dippa (290) weaves giant cream letters behind a figure and in front of a bowl. The type is architecture and the food lives inside it. This is the most promising of the three for a product that has one action to show.
languages.relations: Needs Macro texture and the drawn overlay or Two-color spot illustration to exist. The opposite of Reductive packaging, where type never touches the image.

languages.title: Two-color spot illustration
languages.define: One line weight, one or two flat inks, halftone or stipple for tone. The drawing of the mid-century cookbook and the instruction leaflet.
read: This is the printed kitchen. Numbered steps drawn in pink and green (076), a red pot on green tile cut in lino (137, 153), stacked enamel pots in a folk pattern (077), a sandwich exploded into floating layers (095). The line is even and unhurried, the fills are flat, and shading, where there is any, is a screen of dots. The reference is the two-color spot illustration of 1950s cookbooks and the process diagrams on the back of a box.

The pot is a token of this language rather than a subject. Drawn this way it signals the domestic kitchen of a particular era: enamel, flowers, steam as a curl. When the type is hand-carved to match (137), the whole image reads as one print. Graza's man and olive (132) do the same in the register of a 1940s newspaper ad.

What the language does to tone: it makes instruction friendly. The same steps set in photographs would be a manual; drawn in two inks they are an invitation. It also keeps the food generic (a tomato, a pot), which is why the brands on the board pair it with a photograph when the food itself needs to be seen.
languages.relations: The natural partner of Condensed caps and label typography for instructions. Its opposite in illustration is Botanical illustration: the same subjects, a different claim.

languages.title: Botanical illustration
languages.define: Produce painted or drawn as a specimen: watercolor, gouache, engraving. The seed packet and the horticultural plate.
read: A tomato cut in half in watercolor (330), heirlooms in a loose gouache (098), a radish on a kraft packet (203) and the same radish embroidered (204). The drawing attends to the particular fruit, its skin and seeds, with the care of a catalog. The reference is the seed packet, the canning label with a painted beet (185) and the botanical plate.

The claim this makes is about the ingredient, not the brand: this is what goes in. It is the opposite of two-color spot illustration, which keeps food generic. Fond's label (185) shows how it sits inside a pack: the painting at the center, bands and gold rules around it, the typographic furniture of the 1940s grocer.
The register is slow. It reads well on a single pack and in print, less well as a system, which is why it appears on the board mostly as single pins rather than as ranges.
languages.relations: Opposes Two-color spot illustration in what it claims about the food. Sits inside Grocery vernacular devices when it appears on a label.

languages.title: Cut-paper illustration
languages.define: Flat shapes with no outline. Color does the modeling. After Matisse's cut-outs, through the mid-century poster.
read: The cookbook cover Food & More Food (001) is the clearest case. Hands and produce are cut from five flat colors, each shape given one soft airbrushed cue of volume and nothing else. Black marker squiggles run across the shapes and off the cover onto the backdrop. The title is a stacked geometric display face with sliced counters, set as a solid block in the lower right. Three registers work together: the cut shape, gestural and warm; the marker line, quick and personal; the architectural type, which holds still while everything else moves.

Lentiful (218, 219) uses the same method as a system: vegetables cut from flat color, laid on a band of flavor color, repeated across a range. Mmm (250) sets cut leaves on dark green under a word. Oxente (002, 310) reduces produce to one-ink silhouettes and makes them a pattern. The cut shape is quick to read, cheap to print, and survives at any size, which is why it travels from poster to pouch without changing.
The language is cheerful by construction. Without outlines there is no drawing to be good or bad at; the color relationships do all the work, and strong, simple contrasts read as optimism.
languages.relations: Shares a lineage with Two-color spot illustration but refuses the line. When the figure gets a face it becomes Character illustration.

languages.title: Character illustration
languages.define: A cast that performs the food: rubber-hose mascots at one end, naive one-line vegetables at the other.
read: The board carries two character traditions and they make opposite claims. The rubber-hose mascot (007, 212, 319) is polished: round limbs, gloves, a grin, the 1930s cartoon that became the standard of American food advertising. It promises craft and a brand with a history. The naive vegetable (206, 208, 151) is one line, one color, barely a face; it promises sincerity and a brand that does not take itself seriously.

The interesting work is in the middle. Long Weekend (043, 165, 182) puts a photograph of the soup in a frame and lets cartoon vegetables walk around it, so the photo is a window in a cartoon world. Then it reverses the trick (251, 164): an onion character lounges in the real cup with real water poured on it. The drawing sits on the photograph like a sticker, never entering its space, and that refusal is the joke. Bowl'd (241) makes the cast a system, one vegetable per tile, one tile per flavor.

What a character does to a pack is set its audience. The more finished the drawing, the more it reads as for children or as nostalgia for having been one. The looser the line, the more it reads as an aside between adults.
languages.relations: Joins Macro texture and the drawn overlay and Styled lifestyle photography in the hybrids, where a drawing sits on a photograph.

languages.title: Psychedelic collage and retro print
languages.define: Cut photographs, airbrush, chrome, halftone and off-register ink: images that are about a printed past.
read: Pasta Dreams (091) is the fullest example. Photographic cut-outs of spaghetti, breadsticks, a tomato and a chili are arranged on a sky of clouds and orange swirls; a fork lifts a nest of pasta over a checkerboard floor; bubbles drift. The lettering is a 1970s bubble script. The sensibility is specific: the cut-out animation of Terry Gilliam, the Italian-kitsch advertising of the 1970s, food made monumental and placed on a stage. It is camp with appetite, and the collage is what makes the appetite theatrical rather than documentary.

Around it sit the other retro prints. Chrome bubbles on a dark field (113) and the Dior card (014) are 1980s airbrush. Oh What Fun (138) is a 1960s greeting card with drop shadows and sparkles. Brilliant (021) is Pop's detergent box in four colorways. Vybes (081) marbles fruit like endpaper. Strangers (105) blurs its color into soft blobs. These share a wish to look printed, or filmed, in a decade other than this one.

The register is the most purely nostalgic on the board, and the most dangerous for a new product: it tells you what era the brand admires before it tells you what the product is. On the board it belongs to posters, title cards and limited editions, almost never to a shelf pack.
languages.relations: The most self-aware language here. Its print textures turn up quietly inside Heavy soft display type and Two-color spot illustration.

languages.title: Macro texture and the drawn overlay
languages.define: Food photographed close enough to become a surface. Then, in a few pins, a drawn line laid on that surface.
read: At this distance the food stops being a dish and becomes a material: noodles filling the frame (096), stew with beads of oil (097), cherries in ice (101), a bitten pastry with sprinkles (196). The language of appetite in contemporary food photography is texture at macro, and the board collects it without packs attached. Nine broth cups from above (184) take the same interest and turn it into a typology: foam, oil, a lemon wheel, each cup a different surface.

The hybrids are where this becomes useful. TOMATO (094) sets thin type on a sauce macro. The tomato purée with a tiny line drawing (089) does something stranger: the texture supplies seriousness and hunger, the line drawing supplies scale play and a shrug. The drawing sits on top like a sticker and refuses to be in the photograph's space, so the image is affectionate rather than gourmet. Broth with handwritten ingredient labels (133) and mac and cheese with round stickers (294) do the same with words. The combination lets a brand be appetizing and light at once, which neither register manages alone.
The cost is clarity about the product. Macro texture is generic by nature; without a pack or a line, a noodle macro belongs to anyone.
languages.relations: Its hybrids join it to Character illustration and Type integrated with the food. Color-field product photography is its opposite in distance.

languages.title: Color-field product photography
languages.define: The pack on a stage of one color, hard light, one shadow. From a single hero to a family tiled across the frame.
read: This is the studio language of the 2010s and 20s: a pack set on seamless paper in one color, lit hard from one side so it throws a single shadow, the room matched to the pack (047, 224: red cups, red tomatoes, red wall). Sometimes the room is a floor of tile (092, 300, 314) or a gradient (064, 260). The product becomes a sculpture and the color becomes the mood.

Within this language the main variable is number. Nufs alone on sky blue (064) is a monument. Ollie's pair (033, 107) is a conversation. Nooish's cups laid in rows on a slant (254) and Pick Up's wall of boxes (022) are a pattern, the supermarket shelf-blocking rebuilt as a picture. The nine broth cups (184) take the idea to a typology, where the arrangement matters more than any single object.

The language favors brands with a color-per-flavor system, because the set can change with the pack. It is also where most of the board's monochrome pins live: one hue over pack, prop and ground reads as control, and control reads as a brand.
languages.relations: Hosts most of the color-per-flavor systems. Opposes Ingredient still life, where the set is a real room.

languages.title: Ingredient still life
languages.define: The pack among its raw ingredients, in a real or convincing room: the plinth of garlic, the tomato on the can, the lunch table.
read: Where the color-field set controls everything, this language lets the room in. A hummus tub on a heap of garlic against yellow tile (247). A tomato balanced on a pair of bone-broth cans (186). A mayonnaise bottle on a plate with pickles and dill (263). Lentil cups on a table with the beans and peppers that went into them (221). The ingredient is placed beside the pack as evidence, and the light is warmer and softer than in the studio.

The composition is the still life: a few objects, a surface, a cloth. It reads as editorial rather than retail, and brands use it for the feed and the billboard rather than the shelf. The ramen bowl on red tile with a sachet beside it (166) and the lunch on a striped tablecloth (258) show how far the pack can recede before the picture stops being about it.
The claim is simple and strong: this is food, here is what is in it. For a product whose contents are the point, this is the language that proves them.
languages.relations: Opposes Color-field product photography in control. Shares the ingredient-first claim with Botanical illustration.

languages.title: Styled lifestyle photography
languages.define: People in a staged everyday moment, shot with direct flash or bright daylight, wardrobe and props in the brand's colors. The product is one prop in the scene.
read: Ayoh's mayo goes straight from the bottle into a mouth at an open fridge, lit by a flash that flattens the room into color (259). Lazy Food's pouch is held against striped pajamas (257). Long Weekend's cups are stacked against a denim shirt drawn over with vegetables (252). The pictures borrow from 1970s and 80s family snapshots and from fashion editorial, and the styling is exact: the wardrobe matches the pack.

The tone is candid, but nothing is accidental. The person is mid-gesture (eating, pouring, carrying), the props are chosen for color, and the product sits where the eye lands. It is the language of the feed and the campaign, rarely of the pack itself.

What it adds is a person and an occasion: a late snack, a slow morning, a picnic. What it costs is the food, which is often barely visible. The brands that use it best pair it with a drawn layer or a large line of type, so the brand survives the scene.
languages.relations: Shares subjects with Demonstration photography but not its purpose. Pairs with Character illustration when a drawing is laid over the scene, and with Copy-led design when a line of type is.

languages.title: Demonstration photography
languages.define: The product's action, photographed: a pour, a drip, a melt, a dissolve.
read: Cometeer built a brand on this language. A dark puck sinks in a glass mug in hard light against a two-color ground (315); a capsule tips into a glass of ice (316). The format is one nobody has used, and the photograph explains it in a single frame: clear glass so the change shows, flat color so nothing competes with it.

Elsewhere the action is a pour or a drip borrowed from older advertising: root beer falling as a rope into a glass of ice (268), cheese running off a pouch onto a plinth (106), candy melts dripping down a green bag (237), sauce poured into paper cups (232). These are the appetite shots of soda and snack advertising since the 1950s, reset on seamless color.

Transformation is the rarest subject on the board. Two images show something dissolving, and both are Cometeer. For a product that disappears into the pot, this is the thinnest language here and the one most directly about what the product does.
languages.relations: Needs Macro texture and the drawn overlay or Color-field product photography as its ground. The only photographic language about what a product does rather than how it looks.

languages.title: Grocery vernacular devices
languages.define: The supermarket's own furniture, quoted: bursts, ovals, seals, price stickers, bands and gold rules.
read: A third of the board carries something that looks stuck on afterward. A "Yes!" sticker on an apple (169), three Hato ovals in three colorways (211), a navy burst on a can, a painted tray of tomatoes with its price labels (193). These are not decoration; they are the grammar of the grocery store, and using it is a way of claiming a place on the shelf before the pack is on one.

Two generations are visible. The older one is the label: Heyday's cans (222, 223) and Fond (185) rebuild the 1940s canning label with bands, seals and a painted ingredient; Nooish (226) does it with a bowl window and "Instant Classic!"; Ramen is Love (341) is a 1950s Japanese-American wrapper. The newer one is the sticker: a claim in a pill, a burst or a cloud, tilted, as if applied by a person (231, 293). The first says we have always been here; the second says we just arrived and we are friendly.
The vernacular is where label typography gets its shapes. It is also the easiest language on the board to overdo: once a pack has four bursts it is a coupon.
languages.relations: Supplies the shapes of Condensed caps and label typography. Shares the quotation habit with Script lettering and Psychedelic collage and retro print.

languages.title: Translucency and windows
languages.define: Seeing the food through the pack: die-cut windows, clear bags, frosted film, jelly, a sheet held to the light.
read: The board wants to see inside. Dally's pouch (063) is white with the peach jelly spheres showing through. Lumi's wrapper (100) cuts a window around the candy. Onigiri (174) is wrapped in printed film with the rice visible. Rocca (324) sets translucent jelly shapes into a gray box like gems. A sachet of blooming tea shows the flower through a round window (178).

Then there are the material pins, which have no brand at all: a clear, seed-flecked sheet held to the light (331), leaves sealed in an edible film (332), tinted translucent sheets cut by hand (177). These are the closest things on the board to the product itself, and they are photographed as objects of wonder rather than as packaging.

Translucency is a claim of trust by sight, and it is also an aesthetic: the sugared jelly cubes (197, 198) and the frosted pouches (109) glow because light passes through them. A language that works best when the food is beautiful and worst when it is not.
languages.relations: The only language that touches the product's own material. The carton of Structural and conceptual packaging tells; the window shows.

languages.title: Structural and conceptual packaging
languages.define: Structure that means something: a carton drawn as an oven, a box that folds into a tray, a lid printed on the inside.
read: A box printed as an oven with cartons stacked inside it (115). A line of microwave boxes with the timer at 1:30 (190). A seed box that folds into its own husk tray (322). A T-shirt sold in a cereal box with a word search on the back (118). These packs are jokes about packs, and the lineage is Pop: Warhol's Brillo boxes made the supermarket carton a sculpture, and these make the carton a prop.

A quieter version prints the inside. Graza's mailers (325, 327) carry a drawing and a line on the inner lid. Basao's tea sachets are filed in a kraft box like index cards (333). Blooming tea (178, 180) sells a box with a window and a glass teapot beside it. The structure does the storytelling and the outer graphics can stay plain.

Pick Up's back panel (283), "collect all six flavors" with a how-to-enjoy strip, is the cereal box's own grammar reused on a biscuit. The pack as a thing to read, keep or play with is a different promise from the pack as a sign, and it is the one that survives the unboxing.
languages.relations: Pairs with Reductive packaging when the structure carries the idea. Opposes Translucency and windows.

languages.title: Reductive packaging
languages.define: Minimal surface, small type, plain material. The pack that lets the object or the material speak.
read: A green coffee pouch with a tiny white label (109). White pet-food sachets with a line drawing and nothing else (285). An apricot and a pear on gray with three spaced words, FOOD AS ART (093, 117). A tomato can with a plain painted label among loose tomatoes (191). These pins are the board's quiet, and they are quiet by subtraction: no burst, no character, no color field.

Two sources: the specialty-coffee pouch, which inherited its reticence from Japanese stationery, and the still-life photograph of the museum catalog. Both ask the viewer to look at the thing rather than the sign. Rose's boxes (303, 235) belong here too: a pattern taken from the food, an emboss, and type small enough to be missed.

The language is a position. On a shelf of heavy display type and bursts, the plain pack reads as expensive, and the material (kraft, frosted film, uncoated board) has to be good enough to carry that reading.
languages.relations: Defined by refusing Heavy soft display type, Character illustration and Grocery vernacular devices. Shares an interest in material with Translucency and windows.

visual_tensions.title: Photographed food vs drawn food
visual_tensions.text: A macro promises taste; a drawing promises charm. Where both appear, the drawing sits on the photograph as a remark (089, 251).

visual_tensions.title: Quoted tradition vs new voice
visual_tensions.text: One rebuilds an old label straight; the other drops the quotation and lets the copy carry the brand.

visual_tensions.title: Display type vs label type
visual_tensions.text: Every pack sets a proportion between the two, and the proportion decides whether it reads as a toy or a specification.

visual_tensions.title: Showing vs telling
visual_tensions.text: A clear wrapper proves the food by sight; a printed carton has to say what is inside.

visual_tensions.title: One pack vs the range
visual_tensions.text: A single pack on a field has to hold alone; a range tiled to the edges has to work as a unit.

visual_tensions.title: Polished vs naive
visual_tensions.text: A finished cartoon cast and a one-line vegetable make opposite claims about craft and do the same job: they carry the personality so the photograph can stay plain.

visual_tensions.title: Controlled set vs real table
visual_tensions.text: One hue over pack, prop and wall reads as control; lunch on a striped cloth reads as trust.

brand_studies.name: Cometeer
brand_studies.sells: DTC flash-frozen coffee: a brewed puck in an aluminum capsule that melts into hot water, ice or milk.
brand_studies.effect: a near-future appliance brand with a 1960s warmth
synthesis: Cometeer sells a format nobody has used: coffee as a frozen puck. The identity's job is to make that feel like an old favorite. A connected cream script with a swash underline, closer to a 1960s airline or motel sign than to a coffee roaster, carries the warmth. Everything around it speaks the language of an appliance: small condensed caps, three icons, the instruction "melt, mix, enjoy" set in a ring.

Color is the only variable. One saturated hue per coffee, with the photograph and the wordmark fixed, so a freezer wall reads as a range of coffees rather than a range of designs, and each roaster's own logo sits inside the frame as a guest. The photograph on the box shows the capsule pouring into a hot mug and an iced glass at once: the product explained in one image.
Together, a near-future product with mid-century manners. The novelty reads as quality rather than gadgetry, and the system grows by adding colors, not designs.

brand_studies.name: Rose
brand_studies.sells: Flower-rosin cannabis edibles: sugared fruit cubes (Delights), chocolate, capsules and topicals, made with chefs and California farms.
formula: a flat box, one color per effect
a pattern taken from the food
cubes stacked on the thing they taste of
brand_studies.effect: a cannabis brand that reads as a chef's confectionery
synthesis: Rose is built like a restaurant, not a dispensary. The vocabulary is seasonal fruit, named chefs, farms, and the design follows: the box is a blank field in one color per effect (cream, orange, yellow, pink), with a small uneven "delights" mark and two lines of tiny caps. It behaves like a pastry box. The premium is carried by finish, emboss and spot gloss, and by fronts made from the food itself: raised white circles for boba, glossy seeds on matte red for watermelon. The pattern says ingredient before it says brand.

Photography stacks the cubes on the object that names the flavor or the effect, an apple, a melon, a clock, a cloud, in shallow focus against one color. The CGI renders of capsules and rosin extend the same idea toward science without leaving the pastry register. On screen the type is a grotesk and a Century, and the pages teach process rather than sell.
Together: minimal graphic surface, maximal material finish, food-first imagery. The brand's restraint is what makes a product most states regulate read as a thing from a good kitchen.

brand_studies.name: Stiller's
brand_studies.sells: Low-sugar soda in classic flavors: Lemon Lime, Root Beer, Shirley Temple, Shirley Cola.
formula: a metallic can, one color per flavor
an upright joined script running up the can
brand_studies.effect: the 1950s fountain sign reproduced exactly so the joke can be told straight
synthesis: The design is a pastiche with perfect fidelity. The joined script runs up the can like a wall sign; the can is metallic in one flavor color; the claims sit in navy bursts with white slab type ("Only 30 Calories!", "No Biotics!"); a boast in bold italic serif crosses the top. This is the grammar of mid-century soft-drink advertising, reproduced without irony on the can, so that the irony can live elsewhere.

Elsewhere is the copy and the film. "It's a soda for your mouth." "Made by 100% real human celebrity people." The celebrity founder is the punchline of his own brand, and the launch film parodies old soda ads. The imagery stays cold and literal: condensation beads, cans on a block of ice, a rope of root beer into a glass, each on a gradient of its own color.
Together: the straighter the can, the funnier the voice. A design that quoted loosely would have had to carry the joke itself; this one carries only the quotation, and the quotation is immaculate.

brand_studies.name: Sorry Nonna
brand_studies.sells: Australian jarred pasta sauce with rewritten classics: Spicy Gochujang, Zesty Limoncello, Creamy Vodka, Miso & Garlic.
formula: wide caps with an offset shadow
brand_studies.effect: a label that holds the straight face while the flavor name winks
synthesis: The label borrows the Italian tinned-tomato canon: bands, gold rules, wide display caps, primary colors, a brand line that wraps the jar ("We stole the recipe and made it better"). Everything on it is the tradition except one line, the flavor, and that line is the whole joke. Gochujang in an arrabbiata, limoncello in a marinara. The design never smiles, which is why the name can.

The system is one layout with a colorway per flavor and gold as the constant. Claims are red line icons on yellow discs inside a dashed ring, an angry nonna among them. The jar is photographed straight on against a gradient of its own label color, or in front of its own name set very large, or on gingham among older women cast as the nonnas. The site keeps the voice up ("Nonna would be appalled" in an empty cart).
Together: a brand in which the design is the authority and the copy is the rebellion, in equal measure, on every surface.

brand_studies.name: Alec's Culture Cup
brand_studies.sells: Single-serve probiotic ice cream under a crackable dark-chocolate shell, from Alec's Ice Cream (A2 dairy, regenerative farms).
formula: a brown soft serif larger than the parent name
one pastel per flavor, brown constant
a cast drawn in the flavor's darker tone
brand_studies.effect: a health product in the grammar of a treat
synthesis: The product has one action and the front shows it: the cup with its shell broken and a spoon going in. The sub-brand name, Culture Cup, is set larger than the parent in a brown soft serif with ball terminals, with "probiotic ice cream" arched over it, a cereal-box hierarchy. The parent's 2022 system is carried over underneath: the lowercase wordmark, a line-drawn cow and earth, a pastel per flavor.

Brown holds everything. It is the lettering, the shell and the constant across six pastels, so the range reads as one product in six flavors rather than six products. Characters drawn in each flavor's darker tone (cow, globe, sun) do the regenerative story without a paragraph; the numbers (140 calories, 10 g sugar) sit in corner tiles because the product is a portion and the portion is the promise.
Together: a health claim dressed as dessert. The shell is both the hero image and the reason brown can be the system's constant.

brand_studies.name: Wobble
brand_studies.sells: DTC gelatin dessert mix: grass-fed gelatin, fruit juice powders, collagen. Strawberry, Sour Berry, Mango.
formula: a rounded lowercase wordmark laid over it
a narrow bouncy serif for titles
a maze on the side, stickers in the box
brand_studies.effect: a nostalgia product that does not look nostalgic in the old way
synthesis: The box front is a photograph of the molded jelly in its flavor color with the off-white rounded wordmark laid across it on a pale ground. The wordmark and the jelly share a silhouette, the mold, so the mark and the product become the same shape; the second logo lockup makes that literal by putting the word inside a red jelly-mold form. The retro references are carried by the type system rather than by texture: a narrow bouncy serif ("Friend") for titles, a soft rounded sans for subheads, a monoline script for asides, claims set in cut shapes that are themselves jelly molds.

Color is a named set of six, one per flavor plus accents, and the flavor color fills the field behind each box. The pack carries play on every panel, a maze on the side under "While you wait," four numbered steps on the back, a puffy sticker sheet and a jigsaw as extras, which is the positioning ("Play with your food") made into things.

Photography keeps to two scenes: jellies among toys in a flat lay, and one jelly on a cake stand with a cherry, both in soft even light. Together: a brand whose mark, product and claim shapes are all the same object, which is what lets it be bright without being loud.

method: Pinterest states 341 pins for the board. 341 were captured at the largest size Pinterest holds, in board order, and each was opened and read. Twenty-two are byte-identical repeats of other pins and keep their own numbers. Seven are video pins, read from their cover frames.

The nineteen languages were formed on a second reading of every pin, by how each image is made and what carries its identity, then checked against the per-pin notes so that every pin sits in at least one language. Plates and dials were chosen for range, not frequency.

Makers are named only where the pin's source page or a search confirmed them. Lineage notes (Cooper Black 1922, Matisse's cut-outs, Brillo boxes 1964, rubber-hose animation) are comparisons by eye unless a source is linked.
